article_title: Content-Focused Coaching — Whole Class
citation: Content-Focused Coaching. (2023). Content-Focused Coaching. Evidence for ESSA. https://www.evidenceforessa.org
title: Question-the-Author literacy pattern: students question texts and challenge each other's interpretations
description: The literacy strategies used in CFC are drawn from Question the Author: teachers pose questions to students to promote understanding, interpretation, and active response. Students are encouraged to challenge each other's interpretations and to challenge the authors, identifying places in texts where they want to know more. This pattern positions students as active interrogators of text meaning rather than passive recipients.
requirements: Teachers learn to pose questions to students to promote understanding, interpretation, and active response
target_learning_goals: Text understanding, interpretation, and active response
examples: Students identify places in texts in which they want to know more and challenge each other's interpretations during CFC-supported literacy lessons.

article_title: Improving Chicago's Schools
citation: Luppescu, S., & Hart, H. (2005). Improving Chicago's Schools 2005 Survey Report: Details of Student and Teacher Responses. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://www.consortium-chicago.org
title: Quartile-benchmarked category reporting format compares a school's responses to bottom- and top-quartile schools with defined category descriptions
description: Each measure is reported as a horizontal bar figure showing the percentage of respondents endorsing each survey item, with a diamond marking the systemwide average, followed by a frequency distribution placing the school's responses among four defined categories alongside bottom-quartile and top-quartile schools. Schools are divided 'into four equally sized categories (quartiles) based on their responses to each set of questions,' and each category (e.g., minimal, limited, moderate, extensive) is defined in detail in an accompanying table. Bars exceeding 65 percent extend to the top of the axis without a value label.
requirements: A sufficient response rate for the school and item-level response counts to compute percentages
constraints: The schools in each quartile varied for every set of questions, so a school can be top quartile on one measure and bottom quartile on another; bars above 65 percent are not given value labels
target_learners: school principals, teachers, and Local School Councils conducting self-assessment
target_learning_goals: interpreting school climate and instructional program measures
examples: For Teacher Influence, the report explains that 23 percent of teachers in bottom-quartile schools considered their influence minimal, compared with 4 percent in top-quartile schools and 9 percent in the sample school
key_sources: Luppescu, S., & Hart, H. (2005). Improving Chicago's Schools 2005 Survey Report: Details of Student and Teacher Responses. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/improving-chicagos-schools-sample-high-school-details-2005

citation: Herman, R., Dawson, P., Dee, T., Greene, J., Maynard, R., Redding, S., and Darwin, M. (2008). Turning Around Chronically Low-Performing Schools: A practice guide (NCEE #2008-4020). title: Make visible improvements early in the turnaround process (quick wins)
description: Early in a turnaround, the school should pursue a goal that is important, achievable quickly, and visibly improved, because quick wins "can rally staff around the effort and overcome resistance and inertia." The strategy should be implementable quickly, for example when the school already has the authority and resources to act.
requirements: Start with a goal that is important, can be achieved quickly, and will provide visible improvement, with a strategy the school can implement quickly
constraints: Signaling change without following through with quick wins could make school staff skeptical
target_learners: students and staff in chronically low-performing K-12 schools
target_learning_goals: building staff commitment and momentum for schoolwide improvement
examples: Common quick-win goals named in the guide include changing the school's use of time, improving access to resources and physical facilities, and improving discipline

article_title: The Role of Micro-Credentials in Lifelong Learning and Development: Empowering Learners, Empowering Organizations
citation: Galindo, M., Fennelly-Atkinson, R., Franklin, K., Luna, C. (2024, August). The Role of Micro-Credentials in Lifelong Learning and Development: Empowering Learners, Empowering Organizations. Digital Promise. https://doi org/10 51388/20 500 12265/225
title: Six design characteristics of rigorous and meaningful micro-credentials
description: The eBook enumerates the characteristics that distinguish the most rigorous and meaningful micro-credentials from lower-quality offerings. They are "Competency-based", articulating a discrete skill and the evidence required; research-backed; personalized, letting learners choose credentials aligned to their goals and pace; on-demand; shareable on resumes and profiles; and recognizing, honoring skills "regardless of when, how, and where they were attained", including prior learning. The pattern cautions that quality varies across the field, so these characteristics serve as design and selection criteria.
requirements: Each micro-credential must articulate a discrete skill, the specific evidence to submit, and be grounded in research illustrating how the competency supports positive professional impact
constraints: The quality of micro-credentials varies; these characteristics describe the most rigorous and meaningful subset
target_learning_goals: Recognition of specific, in-demand skills aligned to career goals
examples: Digital Promise's own credentials embody the pattern, being individually assessed by a subject matter expert and awarded as Open Badges with secure metadata

article_title: Preschool Quality and Child Development: How Are Learning Gains Related to Program Ratings?
citation: Sussman, J., Melnick, H., Newton, E., Kriener-Althen, K., Draney, K., Mangione, P., & Gochyyev, P. (2022). Preschool quality and child development: How are learning gains related to program ratings? Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/422.974
title: Quality Counts California (QCC) quality rating and improvement system
description: Quality Counts California is a quality rating and improvement system, a collaboration between First 5 California, the California Department of Education, and the California Department of Social Services. Early learning and care sites are rated on seven elements and assigned a final quality rating in a tiering system ranging from Tier 1 (lowest) to Tier 5 (highest). The seven elements are child observation; developmental and health screenings; lead teacher qualifications; teacher–child interactions; teacher–child ratios and group size; program environment rating scales; and director qualifications, with ratings assigned by trained assessors based on program documentation and classroom observations. Participation is voluntary; 28% of licensed early learning centers participated during the 2020–21 funding year.
requirements: Ratings are assigned by trained assessors based on program documentation and classroom observations
constraints: Participation in QCC is voluntary
target_learners: preschool children ages 4.5 to 5.5 in publicly funded early learning programs
target_learning_goals: early learning and development across social-emotional, language and literacy, and mathematics domains
examples: The study analyzed QCC ratings alongside DRDP scores for approximately 70,000 children in 1,700 rated programs

article_title: Corequisite Remediation in Mathematics: A Review of First-Year Implementation and Outcomes of Quantway and Statway
citation: Strother, S., & Klipple, K. (2019). Corequisite remediation in math: A review of first-year implementation and outcomes of Quantway and Statway. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://carnegiemathpathways.org/reports/
title: Quantway College with Corequisite and Statway College with Corequisite one-term course sets
description: Two one-term course sets developed by the Carnegie Math Pathways for corequisite remediation, each pairing a college-level course with a developmental-level corequisite. As the report describes them, "Each is designed as a one-term stand-alone course set: a college-level course with some embedded learning supports and a corresponding corequisite course that provides learners with additional support." Both courses in each pair use the pedagogy and learning supports of the original two-term pathway courses, and developmental-level lessons were designed to be independent so faculty can skip lessons. Institutions could use separate or single enrollment, and contact hours for the pair ranged from four to six across the six implementing institutions.
requirements: Faculty time before each course pair starts to review lessons, select content, and structure course timelines to fit the local implementation configuration
constraints: Learning must take place in a shorter time frame than the two-term pathways, and faculty reported too little time for student learning as the chief challenge
target_learners: College students placed into developmental mathematics at two-year and four-year institutions
target_learning_goals: College-level quantitative reasoning or statistics credit earned in a single term
examples: Six institutions delivered the offerings via 15 faculty across 21 sections reaching 410 students in spring 2018 and fall 2018

article_title: Investing in Our Nation's Future: Advancing Educational Opportunity for Underserved Students
citation: García, E., Levin, H. (2025). Investing in Our Nation's Future: Advancing Educational Opportunity for Underserved Students. Los Angeles, CA: The Civil Rights Project/Proyecto Derechos Civiles, UCLA. https://escholarship.org/uc/item/29h9c9dn
title: Design education investments with sufficient quality, intensity, duration, and dosage to yield strong benefit-cost ratios
description: The report's economic evaluations indicate that intervention design features drive returns: "the quality, intensity, and duration of the interventions are important, as higher benefit-to-cost ratios are usually associated with more resource-intense programs and those with stronger dosage effects and/or with longer exposure." This principle directs policymakers and program designers to resource interventions adequately rather than scaling back inputs, since under-resourced versions may fail to reproduce the returns documented in evaluations.
requirements: Programs must be funded and implemented at the quality, intensity, and duration levels associated with higher benefit-to-cost ratios in the evaluation literature
constraints: Higher benefit-to-cost ratios are associated with more resource-intense programs, implying greater upfront cost
target_learners: All students, with particular benefit for the most disadvantaged children
target_learning_goals: Maximizing net economic and educational returns on educational investment
examples: The report's synthesis of economic evaluations found stronger dosage effects and longer exposure linked to higher returns.

title: Quality gatekeeping: securing critical stage-gate assessments rather than every task
description: This pattern concentrates heightened assessment security at critical program-level checkpoints such as capstone projects, demonstrations, or milestone evaluations, rather than attempting to secure every assessment against GenAI. The article reports that "securing every assessment task against GenAI is both unrealistic and undesirable; instead, programs should identify critical stage-gates" where security is necessary, enabling earlier detection of learning gaps and consistent program standards.

Coordination across the program rather than unit-level decisions
constraints: Securing every task is described as unrealistic and undesirable
target_learning_goals: Verifying essential knowledge and competencies before progression or graduation
examples: One document described the approach as identifying the key assessment moments at a program level and securing those

description: Question Pot is the chatbot scaffold built for the experimental group: "we built and deployed a custom agent named “Question Pot” on the ChatGLM platform using the GLM-4 model as the chatbot interface". It supported students in generating and refining problems through multiple rounds of dialogic interaction, with questioning functions, linguistic styles, and interface components adapted across three rounds of iteration for the three inquiry topics. article_title: LLM-assisted sentiment analysis for integrated computational and qualitative mixed methods education research: A case study of students' written reflection assignments
citation: Xiomara Gonzalez, Gabriella Coloyan Fleming, Andrew Katz, Maya Denton, Jessica Deters. (2026). LLM-assisted sentiment analysis for integrated computational and qualitative mixed methods education research: A case study of students' written reflection assignments. https://www.google.com/search?q=LLM-assisted+sentiment+analysis+for+integrated+computational+and+qualitative+mixed+methods+education+research
title: Quasi-mixed methods: an LLM-human workflow applying quantitative and qualitative analysis to the same qualitative dataset
description: The article proposes a "quasi-mixed" method in which "our “quasi-mixed” method applies quantitative and qualitative analysis to the same qualitative dataset", extending NLP-human mixed-methods workflows to an LLM-human workflow. It is operationalized as a six-stage pipeline: data familiarization, manual quote extraction, human and LLM-assisted sentiment labeling, human revision of LLM labels, parallel qualitative and quantitative analyses, and interpretation of qualitative findings considering quantitative results. The LLM is treated as an additional individual rater whose discrepancies inform deeper analysis.
requirements: Manually extracted quotes for downstream tasks, since the model's own quote extraction was unreliable
Human review of LLM sentiment labels to resolve discrepancies and ensure analytic coherence
Iterative prompt tuning and Python scripts to automate model inference and track outputs
constraints: Prompt designs are dataset- and context-specific, limiting generalizability across research settings
Upfront technical setup and administrative overhead may outweigh payoff for smaller datasets or single-use analyses
Only open source models were ethically usable because participants did not consent to data sharing with third-party commercial entities
target_learners: Undergraduate engineering students in study abroad programs
Education researchers analyzing qualitative reflection data
target_learning_goals: Cross-cultural communication skills
Critical self-assessment and meaning-making through written reflection
examples: The pipeline was applied to 535 quotations from 51 students across three reflection time points, partitioned by seven student identities and lived experiences, using MetaAI's Llama3 model (8 billion parameters) run locally via the Ollama framework with temperature set to 0

article_title: A Qualitative Model for Reasoning about Path and Support
citation: Abhishek Jaiswal, Zoe Falomir. (2026). A Qualitative Model for Reasoning about Path and Support. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20349
title: Qualitative orientation state vector and transition matrix for stair-blocks
description: Blocks in the model carry a qualitative orientation descriptor: 'The vectorO= (Axis,f,ι)governs the spatial projection and parity of the block via three qualitative operations' — Axis (horizontal/vertical), Reflection (mirroring) and Inversion (flipping). Table 1 enumerates the resulting orientation labels (HN, HM, HNI, HMI, VN, VM, VNI, VMI, RB) with their functional affordances, and Table 2 defines how orientations change under Reflect, Invert and Transpose operations, pruning illegal states such as inverted vertical pillars. The solver uses this matrix to explore valid placements during backtracking.
requirements: Each block must carry a scalar size, unique identifier, orientation state vector and stair indicator
Illegal orientations (e.g., VNI and VMI) must be pruned per game rules
constraints: For rectangular blocks only to-and-fro Horizontal-Vertical state transitions exist
target_learning_goals: reasoning about block orientations and affordances
planning legal placements
examples: Figure 2 schematizes the eight qualitative orientation states for a stair-block, with VNI and VMI marked illegal

article_title: Quality-Conditioned Agreement in Automated Short Answer Scoring: Mid-Range Degradation and the Impact of Task-Specific Adaptation
citation: Abigail Victoria Gurin Schleifer, Moriah Ariely, Beata Beigman Klebanov, Asaf Salman, Giora Alexandron. (2026). Quality-Conditioned Agreement in Automated Short Answer Scoring: Mid-Range Degradation and the Impact of Task-Specific Adaptation. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.07647v2
title: Quality-conditioned fairness: automated scoring must maintain consistent accuracy across the full spectrum of response quality
description: Quality-conditioned fairness is the standard the article proposes for evaluating automated scoring: "the requirement that automated scoring systems maintain consistent accuracy across the full spectrum of response quality". The article grounds it empirically: scoring errors concentrate on mid-range responses "typically produced by students whose knowledge is still developing", who may benefit most from formative feedback, making mid-range inaccuracy a fairness concern rather than mere noise.
requirements: states of knowledge must be detected accurately and equitably so that learners at different current states receive appropriate learning support rather than inappropriate help
constraints: the article shows current few-shot LLM scoring violates this standard in the mid-range; generalizability beyond the two biology items remains to be established
target_learning_goals: accurate and equitable scoring of open-ended scientific explanations
formative feedback targeting partially correct understanding
examples: the article turns mid-range degradation from an unknown bias into a known bias, a step it describes as necessary toward improving fairness in educational AI

citation: Sukjaitham, S., Schaaf, M., Brod, G., & Breitwieser, J. (2026). Adaptivity Makes Feedback Effective: Evidence From AI-Generated Feedback on Children's Plans. Preprint. https://osf.io/4w6rz/overview?view_only=dd3ec8d2878243579a463ccd0d77d723
title: Quality-matched feedback design: LLM adaptive feedback versus expert generic guidance materials
description: The study released a web-based feedback provider system, six scenario-based planning tasks, five expert-written generic guidance versions, a Chain-of-Thought prompt for GPT-4-generated adaptive feedback, and a five-dimension feedback quality rubric (specificity, suggestions, explanation, remarks, formulation). Both conditions were "equivalent in instructional purpose, structure, tone, length, and complexity", differing only in response-contingent adaptation. All materials are publicly available on the OSF.

article_title: When is PBL More Effective? A Meta-synthesis of Meta-analyses Comparing PBL to Conventional Classrooms
citation: Strobel, J., & van Barneveld, A. (2009). When is PBL More Effective? A Meta-synthesis of Meta-analyses Comparing PBL to Conventional Classrooms. Interdisciplinary Journal of Problem-Based Learning, 3(1). https://doi.org/10.7771/1541-5015.1046
title: Qualitative meta-synthesis as a method for reconciling divergent meta-analyses of PBL effectiveness
description: The article's organizing approach is a qualitative meta-synthesis: rather than computing a new pooled estimate, it compares and contrasts the assumptions and findings of existing meta-analyses of PBL. The method treats divergent meta-analytic conclusions as data, explaining apparent contradictions (e.g., retention outcomes) by the type of outcome measured. As the article states, "This study used a qualitative meta-synthesis approach to compare and contrast the assumptions and findings of the meta-analytical research on the effectiveness of PBL."
requirements: Requires a body of existing meta-analyses on the topic whose assumptions and findings can be compared and contrasted
constraints: Conclusions are qualitative syntheses of prior meta-analyses rather than new pooled effect estimates
target_learners: students in PBL and conventional classrooms across disciplines
target_learning_goals: long-term retention, skill development, short-term retention on standardized exams
examples: The synthesis reconciled meta-analytic disagreement by showing PBL advantages on long-term retention, skill development, and satisfaction, and traditional-instruction advantages on short-term board-exam retention.

article_title: Incidental vocabulary learning in a natural reading context: an eye-tracking study
citation: Aline Godfroid, Jieun Ahn, Ina Choi, Laura Ballard, Yaqiong Cui, Suzanne Johnston, Shinhye Lee, Abdhi Sarkar and Hyung-Jo Yoon (2017). Incidental vocabulary learning in a natural reading context: an eye-tracking study. Bilingualism: Language and Cognition, Volume 21, Issue 3. https://doi.org/10.1017/S1366728917000219
title: Quantity and quality of lexical processing jointly drive incremental vocabulary development
description: The article advances an account in which two aspects of lexical processing during reading support incidental vocabulary growth: quantity, indexed by number of exposures, and quality, indexed by total reading time. The authors conclude that "both quantity and quality of lexical processing aid incremental vocabulary development" and that the two "may reveal themselves differently in readers’ eye movement records", so different eye-movement measures capture different aspects of processing.
requirements: Eye-movement records from natural reading of connected text
Vocabulary learning measured for both word form and word meaning
constraints: The account is drawn from a single eye-tracking study in which participants read one authentic novel in two sessions.
target_learners: native and non-native English speakers reading authentic texts
target_learning_goals: incidental vocabulary learning of word form and meaning
examples: Growth curve modeling of eye-tracking data during novel reading linked exposure count to form and meaning learning and total reading time to meaning learning

article_title: Developing evaluative judgement: enabling students to make decisions about the quality of work
citation: Tai, J., Ajjawi, R., Boud, D., Dawson, P., & Panadero, E. (2018). Developing evaluative judgement: enabling students to make decisions about the quality of work. Higher Education, 76, 467–481. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10734-017-0220-3
title: Quality-script development: evaluative judgement grows through staged expertise from analytical to pattern-based judgement
description: The paper hypothesises, drawing on the staged theory of expertise of decision-making (Schmidt and Rikers 2007), that students develop "quality scripts" analogous to illness scripts in medical training. Through repeated exposure to work, consideration of standards, and justification of decisions, knowledge about quality becomes linked and chunked into patterns, so judgement becomes less analytical and more intuitive, with analytical reasoning retained as a safety mechanism for non-fitting problems.
requirements: Repeated practice making evaluative judgements in different situations, with justification of decisions in relation to knowledge and standards
constraints: The account is a hypothesis the authors propose by analogy to medical decision-making expertise, not an empirically tested result
target_learning_goals: developing domain-specific judgement of quality
examples: Medical trainees chunk biomedical knowledge with clinical signs into illness scripts, making decisions less analytical as experience grows

title: Qualify concerns about the long-term impact of academic-media multitasking on adolescent achievement
description: Educators and policymakers should temper alarms that media use during academic activities durably damages adolescent achievement. academic attention

article_title: Quasi-communities: rethinking learning in formal adult and vocational education
citation: Emad, G. R., & Roth, W.-M. (2016). Quasi-Communities: Rethinking Learning in Formal Adult and Vocational Education. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-016-9386-9
title: Quasi-community framework for theorizing learning in formal adult and vocational education
description: A quasi-community is an occasioned, temporally limited community within an educational context, retaining dimensions of communities of practice while abandoning others. The article defines it as "an occasioned, temporally limited community within an educational context that lacks the essentially spatiotemporal nature of relations within true communities." Unlike true communities, it has "no noticeable core and periphery": mastery is relative, dynamically distributed, and any member can act as old-timer or newcomer depending on the task at hand. The framework was developed and illustrated through a case study of mariners in formal certification training.
requirements: A common object/motive shared by members must be realized early for the community to form
constraints: The concept addresses formal adult and vocational settings where classes are administratively formed and disbanded after short periods, so collective memory is temporally limited
target_learners: Adult vocational learners returning to college for certification, e.g. mariners
target_learning_goals: Domain competency development for certification and workplace practice
examples: An eight-week Chart-work and Pilotage course for mariners seeking a watch-keeping certificate of competency

description: A lesson-to-course-level design in which instructor and students collectively co-produce the pedagogy around a shared object/motive. Key moves include early surfacing of motives, group activities with free group choice, storytelling, ungraded tests, turn-taking review, and shifting instructor authority toward facilitation.

An instructor who aligns classroom practice with members' motives and shares hierarchical power

citation: B. Slof, G. Erkens, P. A. Kirschner, J. Janssen, J. G. M. Jaspers. (2012). Successfully carrying out complex learning-tasks through guiding teams' qualitative and quantitative reasoning. Instr Sci 40:623–643. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-011-9185-2
title: Introduce qualitative representations before quantitative ones and let learners construct representations congruent with the tasks to be carried out
description: The article derives two design principles from its findings: to support acquisition of domain understanding, instruction should gradually increase complexity by "introducing qualitative representations before quantitative ones"; and to support application of that understanding, "instruction should allow for constructing representations congruent with the tasks to be carried out". Together these prescribe sequencing tools so each phase's representational guidance matches its part-task demands.

constraints: The authors state there are multiple reasons to assume these design principles do not automatically apply to other domains, learning tasks and settings

citation: F. Egert, R.G. Fukkink, A.G. Eckhardt. (2018). Impact of In-Service Professional Development Programs for Early Childhood Teachers on Quality Ratings and Child Outcomes: A Meta-Analysis. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654317751918

description: The article proposes that improving pedagogical process quality is the pathway through which in-service training affects young children's development. It states that "quality improvement is a key mechanism to accelerate the development of young children," grounded in its finding that child-level effect variance was significantly related to effects on quality ratings (53% explained variance). The framework positions external quality ratings as the proximal outcome and child development as the distal outcome of professional development.

citation: Tim Kühl, Benedict C. O. F. Fehringer, Stefan Münzer. (2022). Unifying the Ability-as-Compensator and Ability-as-Enhancer Hypotheses. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09650-5
title: Analytical approach: regression model with two design dummies and quadratic interaction terms to test the unifying conceptualization
description: The article introduces a multiple regression model in which the aptitude variable enters as a continuous predictor and visual design is coded with two dummy variables, dumOpt and dumSub, each carrying a quadratic interaction term with ability. The relevant coefficients are 'b 41 and b 42 indicating the specific progression of the regression lines presented in Fig. 1', and the five possible coefficient combinations 'can be summarized by the simple hypothesis "b42 > b41" indicating a higher benefit from the optimized visual design than from the suboptimal visual design in the medium ability range'. This approach detects nonlinear interactions that linear moderation tests would miss.

article_title: A scale in ancient history.
citation: Sackett, L. W. (1922). A Scale in Ancient History. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journals/edu
title: Use scale points as a quantitative, not rigidly qualitative, measure of retention in a school subject
description: The article's scale-use method converts class averages per question into fractions of a perfect grade, multiplies each into the question's scale value, and sums the products into total scale points located on a linear scale via subtotals. The article states "Thus, the scale becomes a quantitative rather than a rigidly qualitative measure of ability in these particular aspects of ancient history," comparable with other scales measuring retention after training, and notes it can be made more qualitative by scaling each test separately.
requirements: Pupils take the original tests in whole or in part, work is graded on the basis of 10 per cent per question using the score card, and class averages are found for each question before multiplying into scale values
constraints: The scale measures ability only in these particular aspects of ancient history, and the qualitative and quantitative lapsing of information over time remains to be determined
target_learners: individual pupils and classes in ancient-history courses
target_learning_goals: measuring amount of retention in ancient history after instruction
examples: A class scale grade of 3.6 on question 10 of Test II yields .36 x 151 = 64 scale points; a total of 3200 points places the class between scale values 217 and 219

description: The review defines short answer questions within a hierarchical view of question types organized under three swim lanes: depth of learning, question category, and question type. citation: D. J. Webb. (2012). Improving student's problem-solving ability as well as conceptual understanding without sacrificing the physics content of a class. https://arxiv.org/abs/1210.3385
title: Sequence qualitative thinking on core ideas first, then move to computationally complicated problems later in the term
description: The article recommends organizing a course so students spend considerable early time building qualitative understanding of overarching ideas before tackling algebraically demanding applications. It reports that "students are better prob lem solvers if they have spent considerable time at the beginning of the quarter (or semester) on qualitative thinking before progressing to more computationally complicated problems". In the trial, 60% of homework time stayed conceptual while the 40% devoted to complex problems was moved to the final weeks.
requirements: The course must contain both overarching largely qualitative ideas and "computationally complicated applications of those ideas", which the article says almost every physics class includes.
constraints: Supporting evidence comes from one introductory mechanics comparison at a single university; the author notes there are only glimpses of this general kind of result in earlier education literature.
target_learners: introductory physics students for physical scientists and engineers (undergraduates)
target_learning_goals: problem solving on algebraically complicated physics problems
conceptual understanding of forces and motion
examples: Section I spent the first 6 of 10 weeks on classical ideas connecting forces and motion, then the final 4 weeks applying those principles to the algebraically complicated problems physicists prize.

conceptual understanding of Newtonian mechanics

article_title: Employing real experiments and modern viewpoints in the teaching of modern physics
citation: Muhammad Sabieh Anwar. (2013). Employing real experiments and modern viewpoints in the teaching of modern physics. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/1308.4359
title: Teaching quantum physics through the field viewpoint: the wavefunction as the nonrelativistic limit of a quantum field
description: The course adopted Hobson's framework in which the electron is a quantized field and the Schrodinger wavefunction "is simply stated as the nonrelativistic limit of a quantum ﬁeld". In this view, the field is non-local and extends through space, the word "particle" refers to a local interaction in which the field deposits quantized energy, and matter and radiation are treated symmetrically. The author reports this removed the need for statements like the electron "behaving" like a wave and explains how "the electron can get across nodes" without artificial tunneling arguments.
requirements: Instructors need access to the Hobson framework materials cited in the course and must reorganize traditional wave-particle exposition around fields
constraints: The article notes an alternative viewpoint criticizing the excessive reification of quantum fields (Mermin), and warns that students' habit of "Sticking to particles as the real thing will hamper the assimilation of the concept of quantized ﬁelds"
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of quantum physics
distinguishing quantum uncertainty from everyday uncertainty
examples: The field viewpoint was used to explain single-electron interference, detection as a local interaction such as a beta particle triggering a Geiger Muller tube, and electron diffraction rings shown at course end

article_title: What we can learn about quantum physics from a single qubit
citation: Wolfgang Dür, Stefan Heusler. (2013). What we can learn about quantum physics from a single qubit. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/1312.1463
title: Physical realizations of the qubit: photon polarization, spin, atom position, and ion electronic states
description: The article treats the qubit as an abstract object and presents several laboratory realizations for classroom illustration: photon polarization (|H⟩, |V⟩ with wave plates and a polarizing beam splitter), spin-1/2 particles (Stern-Gerlach apparatus), an atom trapped in a double-well potential, and electronic states of trapped ions or atoms. The authors write: "we discuss various physical realizations of qubits including a spin1/2 particle, the polarization degree of freedom of a photon, the position of an atom in a double-well potential, and the electronic degrees of freedom of an ion or atom." Each realization illustrates certain aspects well but none is free of possible misconceptions.
requirements: Illustrating the abstract qubit properties with several physical realizations in class
constraints: None of the systems is free from possible misconceptions or potential problems in the classroom
For photon polarization, orthogonal states are antiparallel on the Bloch sphere but orthogonal (90°) in the laboratory, which can mislead
target_learning_goals: relating abstract quantum states to physical systems
understanding measurement in different bases
examples: Experiments with single atoms and ions achieve state control and measurement with a fidelity of 99.99%, and entangled states of up to 14 ions have been created

article_title: Ontological Flexibility and the Learning of Quantum Mechanics
citation: Charles Baily and Noah D. Finkelstein. (2014). Ontological Flexibility and the Learning of Quantum Mechanics. https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.8499
title: Student quantum ontologies are best understood within a resources framework as dynamic cognitive processes
description: The article frames ontologies as mental categorizations of concepts, substances and processes, and contrasts two models: stable cognitive structures versus dynamic processes. It argues student quantum ontologies "can be best understood within a resources framework", in which ontologies are "dynamic cognitive processes, emerging in real time through the coordinated activation of conceptual resources (that are in themselves neither right nor wrong)". This framework underpins the paper's analysis of students' contextual switching between particle, wave, blended, and agnostic descriptions of electrons.
requirements: Both perspectives agree that learning of new concepts is mediated, and sometimes hindered, by prior knowledge
constraints: The two perspectives are not entirely incompatible; both allow productively using multiple parallel ontologies for a single concept when the bounds and limitations of each are understood
target_learning_goals: understanding ontological categorizations of quantum entities such as electrons

citation: Charles Baily, Noah D. Finkelstein. (2015). Teaching Quantum Interpretations: Revisiting the goals and practices of introductory quantum physics courses. https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.8503
title: Three named instructional-approach categories for teaching quantum interpretation: Realist/Statistical, Matter-Wave, and Copenhagen/Agnostic
description: The article organizes introductory modern physics instruction with respect to interpretation into three empirically characterized categories. It states "the instructional approach for each of these courses can be characterized as being either Realist/Statistical, Matter-Wave or Copenhagen/Agnostic," based on classroom observations, analysis of course materials, and instructor interviews. The categories describe whether and how instructors attended to interpretive themes, not their personal interpretations, and are illustrated through how each instructor discusses the double-slit experiment with single electrons.
requirements: Categories are assigned from classroom observations, analysis of course materials, and instructor interviews, reflecting whether and how interpretive themes were attended to in teaching.
constraints: The article states the categories "certainly do not encompass all the ways instructors might teach quantum interpretations" and that other perspectives exist without published studies of their learning impacts.
target_learners: Introductory calculus-based modern physics students, primarily engineering majors
target_learning_goals: Understanding the physical interpretation of quantum phenomena and the nature of quantum uncertainty

article_title: Presenting particle physics and quantum mechanics to the general public
citation: J. Strauss. (2014). Presenting particle physics and quantum mechanics to the general public. https://www.projectprakash.org
title: Quantum Bayesian (QBism) view: the wave function describes an observer's judged quantum probability, not an object of reality
description: The article adopts the Quantum Bayesian view, in which "the quantum wave function is a construct serving to describe quantum probability as judged by a specific observer, rather than an object of reality". Quantum probability depends on the observer's informed personal bet, and quantum theory serves to organize those bets; the author quotes it as a theory guiding agents in their interactions with the quantum world. This view underpins the article's advice to present quantum physics as description rather than reified reality.
requirements: Presenters must be able to distinguish descriptive constructs (wave function, operator fields) from objects of reality when answering public questions
constraints: The article attributes this view to cited QBist authors (Fuchs, Mermin) rather than arguing it fully; it acknowledges most of the time the terminus scientist denotes a wider peer group

target_learning_goals: accurate conception of what quantum-theoretical constructs describe
examples: The author answers the public question whether the Higgs field pervades all of space by saying we may talk about the Higgs field if we have in mind an operator field helping to bestow masses to the W/Z bosons

Quantitative questions piloted in free-response form to vet wording, distractors, and reasoning before multiple-choice use

article_title: Teaching Critical Thinking
citation: N.G. Holmes, Carl E. Wieman, D.A. Bonn. (2015). Teaching critical thinking. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1505329112
title: Quantitative comparison tool set with decision tree (t′-score, weighted χ2, residual plots)
description: The experimental curriculum taught a set of analysis tools "used regularly by scientists in any field": the t′-score index comparing two measured values with uncertainty (the difference over the uncertainty in the difference), weighted χ2 for least-squares fitting of data to models, and residual plots showing the point-by-point difference between measured data and a model. Each tool was paired with a decision tree for interpreting outcomes and choosing follow-up actions, such as improving precision when uncertainties may be overestimated or identifying systematic errors when the model appears limited. Procedural tools (histograms, mean, standard deviation, uncertainty propagation) were taught to both conditions.
requirements: Students must be taught both the comparison tools and a framework for using them to decide how to act on comparisons
constraints: A large χ2 might reflect an issue with the model, but students were deliberately not told what to do about it, leaving room for autonomous decision making

A pre-test given after traditional lecture on relevant concepts but before the tutorial

distinguishing individual measurement outcomes from expectation values

citation: Ben Van Dusen and Jayson Nissen. (2020). Associations between learning assistants, passing introductory physics, and equity: A quantitative critical race theory investigation. Physical Review Physics Education Research 16, 010117. https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevPhysEducRes.16.010117

description: A Quantum Interactive Learning Tutorial (QuILT) developed by the authors as a learning tool to help students develop a functional understanding of the corrections to the hydrogen atom energy spectrum due to the Zeeman effect. The article states "We used the difﬁculties as resources in developing a Quan- tum Interactive Learning Tutorial (QuILT)" and that "The initial results from the QuILT are encouraging." The difficulties documented in the written questions and interviews served as the design input for the tutorial.
requirements: Addresses the documented student difficulties with identifying a good basis and applying the two-step DPT approximation
constraints: Only initial results are reported in this article; full evaluation is not described
target_learning_goals: functional understanding of degenerate perturbation theory
finding first-order energy corrections for strong and weak field Zeeman effects
identifying a good basis
examples: The tutorial was developed using the difficulties from 52 undergraduate and 42 graduate student responses and 13 think-aloud interviews as resources

citation: Shaeema Zaman Ahmed, Jesper Hasseriis Mohr Jensen, Carrie Ann Weidner, Jens Jakob Sørensen, Marcel Mudrich, and Jacob Friis Sherson. (2020). Quantum Composer: A programmable quantum visualization and simulation tool for education and research. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.07263
title: Quantum Composer: a node-based drag-and-drop quantum simulation and visualization tool
description: Quantum Composer is an interactive tool where a user connects graphically representable nodes, each corresponding to a physical concept, mathematical operation, or visualization, to build flow-based quantum simulations. It supports one-dimensional single-particle Schrödinger and mean-field Gross-Pitaevskii physics, operator application, expectation values, and quantum optimal control. It is available as a free download for Windows, macOS, and Linux, with tutorial, reference, and exercise pages online.
requirements: Users need onboarding to the interface; the article states exercises are usually not deployed without introductory onboarding to Composer
constraints: Composer allows users to explore a subset of the QEngine's capabilities, one-dimensional single-particle and mean-field physics only
the article notes simulations use dimensionless units with hbar = m = 1 and finite numerical resolution

quantum optimal control
research skills

citation: Mariia Mykhailova and Krysta M. Svore. 2020. Teaching Quantum Computing through a Practical Software-driven Approach: Experience Report. In The 51st ACM Technical Symposium on Computer Science Education (SIGCSE '20). https://doi.org/10.1145/3328778.3366952
title: Quantum Katas: self-paced programming exercises with immediate automated feedback
description: The Quantum Katas are an open-source project of "sets of programming tasks that cover one topic" in quantum computing and Q# programming, designed for self-paced learners. Each kata embeds a testing framework that validates solutions as soon as they are written, using the QDK's full-state quantum simulator, giving immediate automated feedback without access to quantum hardware. Tasks start simple and gradually increase in complexity, building on previous tasks. The course used the katas weekly as a replacement for in-person programming lab time.

Learners need a classical computer; no quantum hardware access is required

quantum computing concepts such as measurements, oracles, and Grover's search

article_title: A Computer Science-Oriented Approach to Introduce Quantum Computing to a New Audience
citation: Özlem Salehi, Zeki Seskir, and Ilknur Tepe. (2021). A Computer Science-Oriented Approach to Introduce Quantum Computing to a New Audience. https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.13552
title: Computer science-oriented approach: quantum computing as a generalization of probabilistic computing taught through linear algebra
description: The framework presents quantum computing "as a generalization of probabilistic and classical computing", abstracting physical concepts through linear algebra so that a quantum state is a vector and quantum gates are unitary matrices. Superposition is introduced "as a property of a unit vector in a Hilbert space" rather than via photon polarization or electron spin, and the material avoids complex numbers entirely, restricted to real numbers. Measurement is described as projection onto two orthogonal planes. This bypasses physics prerequisites, requiring only linear algebra and basic Python programming.
requirements: basic knowledge in linear algebra and introductory programming experience in Python
constraints: the material is restricted to real numbers and does not involve complex numbers
traditional topics such as Deutsch and Bernstein-Vazirani algorithms are purposefully omitted
target_learners: undergraduate and graduate students from STEM-related departments
high school students with programming and linear algebra prerequisites
professionals from diverse backgrounds entering the quantum field
target_learning_goals: basic quantum computing concepts such as qubits, quantum gates, superposition, entanglement
basic quantum programming skills in Python and Qiskit
examples: the Bronze material presents probabilistic states via a game of coin flips and introduces the interferometer as a quantum coin-flipping experiment

article_title: Quanteninformationsverarbeitung in der Gymnasialen Oberstufe
citation: Andreas J. C. Woitzik. (2020). Quanteninformationsverarbeitung in der Gymnasialen Oberstufe. https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.01029
title: Define the qubit as a real vector on the unit circle rather than via the Bloch sphere or complex Hilbert space
description: The unit's central didactic reduction defines a qubit as a two-component real vector with α²+β²=1 on the unit circle, with |0⟩ and |1⟩ corresponding to the classical bit states. The article motivates this because "Für Schüler ist es allerdings verwirrend, dass orthogonale Zustände auf der Kugel Antipoden bilden, also linear abhängig erscheinen," and because the circle suffices for the central phenomena.
requirements: Only real vectors with α²+β²=1 and the two basis states are introduced; no complex Hilbert-space formalism or global-phase discussion is needed.
constraints: The article limits the reduction to the central phenomena of quantum information processing; the Bloch sphere, the standard visualization in physics, is rejected for school use because orthogonal states appear as antipodes on it.
target_learning_goals: representing qubits geometrically and naming the states corresponding to classical bits
examples: The unit introduces |0⟩=(1,0) and |1⟩=(0,1) on the unit circle (Abbildung 2) and lets gates act on this picture.

article_title: Quanteninformationsverarbeitung in der Gymnasialen Oberstufe
citation: Andreas J. C. Woitzik. (2020). Quanteninformationsverarbeitung in der Gymnasialen Oberstufe. https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.01029
title: Introduce quantum gates both as reflections on the unit circle and as truth tables on the basis states
description: A lesson-level design in which one-qubit gates are interpreted geometrically as Drehspiegelungen (reflection-rotations) of the qubit vector on the unit circle — X about the first angle bisector, Z about the horizontal axis, H about the 22.5° axis — which makes gate reversibility immediately evident. Simultaneously the gates are given as truth tables, so that "Somit kann direkt an Bekanntes aus der (klassischen) Informatik angeschlossen werden."
requirements: Truth tables with the basis states are introduced alongside the geometric view to connect to classical informatics.
constraints: For the teaching unit the X, Z and H gates suffice; the rotation R(θ) is given only for completeness.
target_learning_goals: applying simple quantum gates (X, Z, H) to given qubits and understanding gate reversibility
examples: Table I of the article maps |0⟩→|1⟩ under X, |1⟩→−|1⟩ under Z, and |0⟩→|+⟩ under H; the unit also visualizes each gate on the unit circle (Abbildung 3).

article_title: Investigating society's educational debts due to racism and sexism in student attitudes about physics using quantitative critical race theory
citation: Jayson M. Nissen, Ian Her Many Horses, and Ben Van Dusen. (2021). Investigating society's educational debts due to racism and sexism in student attitudes about physics using quantitative critical race theory. Physical Review Physics Education Research 17, 010116. https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevPhysEducRes.17.010116
title: QuantCrit: a quantitative critical race framework for analyzing educational inequities
description: QuantCrit is a quantitative perspective aligned with critical research that the article uses to analyze racism and sexism in physics attitudes. As the article states, "QuantCrit complements qualitative studies by using large-scale data to represent student outcomes in ways that reveal structural inequities that reproduce injustices." The article embodies three principles: the centrality of oppression, categories are neither natural nor given, and data are not neutral and cannot speak for themselves. These principles motivated reporting point estimates and standard errors rather than p values, treating race and gender as social constructs, and reframing outcome gaps as educational debts.
requirements: Large-scale datasets with enough statistical power to model relationships between students' intersectional identities and learning outcomes
constraints: Small samples for intersectional and underrepresented populations can obscure inequities; quantitative measures cannot access all aspects of the educational debts owed by society
target_learning_goals: attitudes about learning and doing physics
equity in physics outcomes
examples: The article used AICc model selection rather than p values and reported point estimates with standard errors, stating this prevented results from focusing solely on well-represented groups

title: Quantum Composer, a drag-and-drop 1D quantum simulation and visualization tool
description: Quantum Composer is an interactive, flow-based programming tool developed at Aarhus University and available for free download, described as "a flexible and interactive tool that enables educators and students to build and simulate one-dimensional quantum systems through a 'drag-and-drop' visual programming and execution interface". Users connect nodes with interactive capabilities and use visualization nodes such as the State Comparison Plot, which can display real part, imaginary part, and probability density of wavefunctions, statically and in time evolution. examples: In the study, students worked through a provided single-well harmonic oscillator flowscene with the Scope feature used to hide unnecessary details

article_title: Intuition in Einsteinian Physics
citation: Schutz, B. (2020). Intuition in Einsteinian Physics. https://scholar.google.com
title: Quasi-Bayesian model-based account of physical intuition
description: The chapter proposes that physical intuition consists of simplified models of the world that win an unconscious, probabilistic competition among alternatives in the brain. Drawing on neural-network-like decision processes and Bayesian statistics, it argues the brain arrives at single decisions using priors from memory, instinct and senses, so "much of what we "think" has been arrived at statistically, not deductively". Intuitions about physics are therefore prescriptions for fitting parts of physics together and for judging what to expect from new experiments. Logic and mathematics are characterised as post-hoc tools for justifying and testing these intuitions.
requirements: Intuitions must be cultivated and then quality-controlled against experiment, observation and challenge from other scientists, since they operate below consciousness
constraints: The author states the identification of intuition with winning unconscious models is "necessarily a simplification"; the brain account is argued from cited neuroscience and philosophy (Gigerenzer 2007; Mercier & Sperber 2019), not tested in this chapter
target_learning_goals: developing physical intuition in Einsteinian physics
understanding the role of intuition versus logic in scientific thinking
examples: The chapter explains detector physicists debugging an instrument by decomposing it into sub-models rather than returning to fundamental equations
key_sources: Schutz, B. (2020). Intuition in Einsteinian Physics. https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.01820

description: Quantum Odyssey is computer software developed by Quarks Interactive that teaches quantum computation through "a visual Plinko (grid of pins) board system where coloured balls travel down the board following different tracks". Players drag picture tiles representing quantum gates (H, X and CTRL) into a circuit panel, and "each picture tile accurately represents a quantum mechanical rule and the player's sequence of tiles is writing a functioning quantum algorithm". constraints: In the piloted version the game "came without narration or explanations", and the article notes the representation can only handle smaller systems compared with real-space alternatives
target_learning_goals: constructing quantum computing algorithms
understanding superposition, interference and entanglement
examples: In the pilot, puzzles 1-3 taught flipping two-qubit arrays, 4-6 superposition, 7-9 reverting superposed qubits to the 00 ground state, and puzzle 10-11 involved constructing and extracting an entangled state

article_title: Introducing Quantum Entanglement to First-Year Students: Resolving the Trilemma
citation: W.M. Stuckey, Timothy McDevitt, Michael Silberstein. (2024). Introducing Quantum Entanglement to First-Year Students: Resolving the Trilemma. https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.12043
title: The pedagogical trilemma for introducing quantum entanglement's mysterious correlations
description: The article names a trilemma facing any physics educator introducing the Bell-inequality-violating correlations of quantum entanglement: compromise completeness by omitting the mystery, compromise satisfaction by telling students the formalism maps to experiments so "there is nothing else that needs to be said," or compromise rigor by venturing into "the metaphysical quagmire of competing QM interpretations." The trilemma resides in the desire for a constructive account, which the authors escape by pivoting to a principle account.
requirements: Applies to introductions of quantum entanglement that confront its mysterious Bell-inequality-violating correlations rather than omitting them
constraints: The article states no experiment can distinguish between metaphysical models and there is no consensus metaphysical model to present
target_learners: first-year physics students for scientists and engineers
target_learning_goals: understanding quantum entanglement and its Bell-inequality-violating correlations
examples: The authors enumerate the three options: omit the mystery, adopt the 'Shut up and calculate!' attitude of the Copenhagen interpretation (42% in a 2011 poll by Schlosshauer et al.), or attempt resolution via competing QM interpretations such as Many Worlds or superluminal pilot waves

citation: Manie Tadayon, Greg Pottie. (2021). Causal Inference in Educational Systems: A Graphical Modeling Approach. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.00654
title: Four-level hierarchy of quasi-experimental designs by control groups, pretests, and time series
description: The article organizes non-randomized educational designs into a four-level hierarchy attributed to Cook, Campbell, and Shadish: "A. Design with no control groups. B. Design with control groups but no pretest. C. Design with control groups and pretest. D. Design for time series data," with D the best. Each level is instantiated with educational examples (one-group posttest, posttest-only nonequivalent groups, pretest-posttest nonequivalent groups, interrupted time series) and a DAG exposing its backdoor paths and internal-validity threats.
requirements: Designs below the top of the hierarchy require attention to threats such as selection bias, regression to the mean, history, and attrition
constraints: The article states ITS, RD, DID, and IV mainly model a single intervention and do not model time-varying treatment-confounder feedback, limiting their fit to education
target_learners: students in educational studies using non-randomized designs
target_learning_goals: estimating causal effects of interventions when randomization is not feasible
examples: Interrupted time series is described as the most powerful design in the hierarchy because many pre- and post-intervention measurements rule out regression to the mean

article_title: Quantum information and beyond -- with quantum candies
citation: Junan Lin, Tal Mor, and Roman Shapira. (2021). Quantum information and beyond — with quantum candies. https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.01402
title: Quantum candies (qandies): a superposition-free pedagogical model for quantum information concepts
description: The qandies model, invented by Kayla Jacobs and greatly expanded here, represents qubits as candies with two general properties, color (red/green) and taste (chocolate/vanilla), where each candy carries only one specific property. The article states: "The key feature of these qandies is that each single qandy really has only a single speciﬁc property." Observing one property destroys the other, illustrating complementarity; non-orthogonal states ground the no-cloning principle; and correlated qandy pairs mimic entanglement as pseudo-entanglement. The model requires no superpositions or mathematics and is extendable to qutrits, the six-state protocol, gates, and non-local boxes.
requirements: A qandy-producing machine with four buttons, one for each specific property {R,G,C,V}, where a user generating the qandy cannot choose more than one specific property
constraints: The model is far from identical to quantum theory: it does not employ superpositions, and some extensions (e.g., unequal numbers of colors and tastes, or four general properties) are not consistent with quantum theory
target_learning_goals: quantum bits
complementarity
no-cloning principle
entanglement
quantum key distribution
examples: Svozil's chocolate-ball staging of BB84 with red- and green-filtering glasses, which the authors show is equivalent to qandies but lacks true quantumness

title: Quantum Picturalism: string-diagram languages (ZX-calculus) as a mathematically rigorous, visually intuitive framework for quantum theory
description: Quantum Picturalism (QP) is a framework for studying, teaching and practising quantum theory through diagrammatic languages. The article states that "QP effects a paradigm shift in how quantum physics is understood and practiced using visually intuitive but mathematically rigorous diagrams, called string diagrams." Its oldest widely adopted language is the ZX-calculus, whose red and green "spiders" with phase angles and wires form the basic building blocks; calculations proceed by graphical substitution rules that preserve meaning. The article claims the rule set is complete, i.e. "suffices to make the ZX-calculus as expressive as the Hilbert space formalism for qubits", so QP can serve as a self-contained descriptive and computational language without linear-algebra prerequisites.

constraints: The article notes completeness is stated for qubits and, via cited work, for arbitrary finite dimension; the educational benefit claims are anticipated and not yet empirically demonstrated in this paper.
target_learners: high-school students aged 16 to 19 without prior quantum physics or advanced mathematics background
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of quantum theory and quantum computing
diagrammatic reasoning and calculation of quantum protocols such as teleportation
examples: The paper works through the quantum teleportation protocol and a CNOT-cancellation proof entirely in ZX-diagrams, and re-expresses the QAOA max-cut algorithm diagrammatically to reveal the network's constraint structure.
